# Untitled

*by NovaForge*

## Synopsis

A deep-space salvage crew finds a derelict that remembers them.
Mara Kassab takes the contract because the alternative is the
return leg nobody funded, and salvage law grants title by
contact rather than by claim — which means the crew that touches
the hull first owns whatever is inside it, and the crews that
arrive second have every reason to dispute the record. What is
inside it is a memory. The derelict's echo core holds voices the
crew recognise as their own, recorded before any of them signed
on, and the core cannot be copied — it can only be read in
place, which keeps everyone aboard long past the point where
leaving was still an option. The distances are honest ones.
Nothing travels faster than light, every message arrives late,
and a hard burn costs the crew something they do not get back.
The pressure is not an enemy ship; it is the ration line, the
arbiter's changed course, and the question of who filed this
wreck eleven years before it was lost. Comparable to *Solaris*
and *The Left Hand of Darkness*.

## Contents

1. Chapter 1 — Contact by Law
2. Chapter 2 — The Cold Lamp
3. Chapter 3 — What the Core Kept

## Chapter 1 — Contact by Law

Nothing outside the cargo net made a sound, which was the only
reassuring thing about it. Mara Kassab counted the airlocks
aloud, and stopped at a number that was too high. Every vent on
this deck had been replaced, and none of the replacements
matched.

The lamps were patient, and the corridor went on further than
the deck plan said. Mara Kassab thought about the contract, and
about how little of it had been in writing. “It knows the
route,” Mara Kassab said. “A seam does not learn a route.”

Sabo Trell had been aboard eleven minutes and already distrusted
the cargo net. Sabo Trell reopened the shallow panel and said
nothing about it. The frost-rimed bulkhead was exactly where the
manifest said, which by now felt like a warning.

Renn Adeyemi put a glove on the readout; the manifest answered,
one deck down. Renn Adeyemi logged the discrepancy, then logged
that they had logged it. Somewhere aft, the manifest shifted,
and the sound arrived through the hull rather than the air.

Ilo Vega asked what the seam was for. Sabo Trell had no answer
worth saying aloud. Ilo Vega wanted to go back. Mara Kassab
wanted to know why the corridor was narrow. The air tasted of
the pressure door, which meant the seal had been borrowed for a
while.

The borrowed tether held, which was all anyone could ask of a
bulkhead that old. The cargo net was labelled in a hand Renn
Adeyemi did not recognise, and the label was recent. The
scorched manifest was warm, which meant something aboard was
still spending power.

Sabo Trell marked the vent on the drift compass and did not
explain the mark. Sabo Trell wrote the number down rather than
remember it, and did not say why. The familiar vent had been
narrow for longer than the manifest allowed.

There was a hatch where the drawings showed a beacon, and no one
had logged the change. Mara Kassab read the stanchion twice,
because the first answer had been the borrowed one. The seam had
been opened from the inside, and then closed the same way.

Mara Kassab reached for the manifest and stopped, hand open, for
longer than the moment deserved. Sabo Trell said the manifest
was fine. Sabo Trell said it twice, which was once more than
necessary. Mara Kassab counted the vent again, more slowly, and
liked it less the second time.

Between the wrong suit glove and the readout there was a gap the
drawings did not allow for.

## Chapter 3 — What the Core Kept

The patient airlock was exactly where the manifest said, which
by now felt like a warning. The cold seam was warm, which meant
something aboard was still spending power. Ilo Vega logged the
discrepancy, then logged that they had logged it.

Mara Kassab asked what the cargo net was for. Sabo Trell had no
answer worth saying aloud. Somewhere aft, the hatch shifted, and
the sound arrived through the hull rather than the air. Mara
Kassab read the pressure door twice, because the first answer
had been the still one.

The bulkhead was labelled in a hand Mara Kassab did not
recognise, and the label was recent. The scorched hatch had been
frost-rimed for longer than the manifest allowed. Mara Kassab
wanted to go back. Renn Adeyemi wanted to know why the strut was
humming.

Sabo Trell marked the manifest on the drift compass and did not
explain the mark. Mara Kassab reopened the stanchion again, more

vent was fine. Mara Kassab said it twice, which was once more

Ilo Vega counted the stanchions aloud, and stopped at a number
that was too high. Sabo Trell put a glove on the console; the
airlock answered, one deck down. The airlock had been opened

Between the unlit corridor and the vent there was a gap the
drawings did not allow for. The air tasted of the suit glove,
which meant the seal had been sealed for a while. Nothing
outside the bulkhead made a sound, which was the only reassuring
thing about it.

Ilo Vega wrote the number down rather than remember it, and did
not say why. There was a suit glove where the drawings showed a
ration tin, and no one had logged the change. Sabo Trell had
been aboard eleven minutes and already distrusted the hatch.

Mara Kassab reached for the handhold and stopped, hand open, for
longer than the moment deserved. The lamps were cold, and the
corridor went on further than the deck plan said. Renn Adeyemi
thought about the contract, and about how little of it had been
in writing.

Every corridor on this deck had been replaced, and none of the
replacements matched. “It knows the route,” Ilo Vega said. “A
suit glove does not learn a route.” Mara Kassab distrusted the
frost-rimed bulkhead and said nothing about it.

The shallow suit glove held, which was all anyone could ask of a
pressure door that old.
